ECE 6390 / Spacecraft systems

Radiation & voting

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows the independent bit faults that a three-channel majority vote can mask.

With three independent channels, each wrong with probability p, a perfect majority voter fails when two or three channels are wrong. Thus PTMR = 3p²(1 − p) + p³ = 3p² − 2p³.

If a separate common-cause event flips all channels with probability q, the supplied model becomes P = q + (1 − q)PTMR. Shared power, clocks, environment, or voter faults require their own treatment.

Voting can mask an individual logic upset. Radiation effects also include cumulative material or device changes and destructive events, for which replicated logic and a perfect-voter probability model are insufficient.

Example

For independent p = 0.01 and a perfect voter, PTMR = 0.000298, or 0.0298%. A common-cause probability sets an additional floor in the extended model.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. If independent channel faults become arbitrarily rare but q = 0.01 remains, what failure probability does the common-cause model approach?

    Let p tend to zero in q + (1 − q)PTMR.

    It approaches q = 0.01, or 1%. Improving independent channels cannot remove the specified shared event.
